name: Eratosthenes' stick and the size of the Earth
scope: A shadow, a well, and the circumference of a planet. T1: around 240 BC, at noon on the summer solstice at Syene (modern Aswan), the Sun stood so exactly overhead that a vertical rod cast NO shadow at all and sunlight reached the bottom of a well (the hook: the shadow that wasn't there). T2: at that same noon, far to the north at Alexandria, a gnomon DID cast a shadow -- Eratosthenes measured the angle at about 7.2 degrees and recognized it as 1/50 of a full circle. T3: so the arc between the two cities is 1/50 of the whole Earth -- 5,000 stadia times 50 = 250,000 stadia (later reported as 252,000, a figure that divides evenly by 60). T4: where the 5,000 stadia came from -- not a survey chain but bematists, professional step-counters paid to pace out distances, plus caravan-day estimates. T4b: the replication rung -- two schools at different latitudes, two vertical sticks, one local noon, and a phone call reproduces the whole measurement today. T5a: how close was he? Nobody knows which stadion he used (estimates run 157 to 185 m), so the Attic value gives about 40,300 km against the true 40,075 km, and the honest claim is 'within a few percent,' not 'he nailed it.' T5b: the geometry hides two cheats -- Syene sits about 37 km north of the Tropic of Cancer and roughly 3 degrees off Alexandria's meridian; the errors partly cancelled. T5c: the world then got SMALLER -- Posidonius' rival figure, adopted by Ptolemy at around 180,000 stadia, shrank the globe for 1,700 years, and it was that undersized Earth Columbus leaned on when he argued Asia was reachable by sailing west. T5d: Eratosthenes' own book On the Measurement of the Earth is LOST -- the method survives only because Cleomedes summarized it centuries later. T3b: the same man ran the Library of Alexandria and invented the prime-number sieve, and rivals nicknamed him 'Beta' -- second-best at everything.
source: Grokipedia 'Eratosthenes' (read in full via browser; grokipedia.com blocks WebFetch with HTTP 403 this session); Wikipedia 'Eratosthenes'. Both trace the method to Cleomedes' later summary rather than to Eratosthenes' lost treatise; both flag the stadion-length ambiguity behind the accuracy claim.
framing_note: The sub-strand's flagship kid-replicable ladder. T1 keys the SHADOWLESS ROD, never a date. Accuracy rail: do NOT assert 'accurate to within 1%' as fact -- the stadion length is unknown, so the honest range is 'within a few percent depending on which stadion he used'; and the well-at-Syene detail comes from Cleomedes' later account, not from Eratosthenes himself. Dinner-test payoff: T4b -- a kid with a stick, a friend a few hundred miles away, and one noon can re-run the whole thing. Distractor mine: real rival ancient numbers (Posidonius' 240,000 and Ptolemy's ~180,000 stadia) and real rival ancient methods (timing a lunar eclipse, star altitude at two ports, watching a ship's hull vanish before its mast) plus real adjacent Alexandrians (Aristarchus, Hipparchus, Archimedes). Anti-restatement: never let the stem say 'the angle is one-fiftieth of a circle' before asking what he concluded -- describe the two shadows and let the inference be recalled knowledge.
history_overlap: geography bank -- the Library of Alexandria and Aswan/Syene as places, and geography's own 'shape and size of the Earth' material. Science keys the shadow-angle METHOD and the stadion ambiguity, NOT the place-tour of Alexandria or the Nile.

name: Cavendish weighs the world
scope: How you weigh a planet in a garden shed. T1: in 1797-98, in a sealed shed on his London estate, Henry Cavendish watched two lead balls pull on each other -- and read the result through a TELESCOPE from OUTSIDE the room, because his own body heat would have stirred the air enough to swamp the signal (the hook: the man who had to leave the room). T2: the apparatus -- a six-foot wooden rod hung on a fine wire with two 2-inch lead spheres on its ends; two 12-inch lead balls of roughly 350 lb each were swung close by an external pulley, and the rod twisted by a few arcminutes. T3: teach density, then key the result -- what Cavendish reported was not a force but the mean DENSITY of the Earth, 5.48 times the density of water. T3b: Cavendish the man -- so severely reclusive that contemporaries said he left written notes for his housekeeper rather than speak to her; Maxwell later worked through his unpublished papers and found he had anticipated Ohm's law and Coulomb's law decades early and told no one. T4a: the mountain came first -- in 1774 Nevil Maskelyne weighed the Earth using Schiehallion in Scotland, measuring how far the peak's own gravity tugged a plumb line sideways (about 11.6 arcseconds) and getting about 4.5 g/cm3. T4b: crunching the Schiehallion survey, Charles Hutton invented CONTOUR LINES to handle the mountain's shape -- a map convention born out of a gravity experiment. T4c: Cavendish never computed G. Newton's law carried a constant of proportionality nobody had measured; the number was extracted from Cavendish's data by later physicists (around 1879, G about 6.75e-11 against today's 6.674e-11). T5a: the arithmetic slip -- his published 5.48 contains an error found decades later; his own data actually give 5.448, within about 1.2% of the modern 5.514. T5b: it wasn't his apparatus. John Michell -- a country rector who also first imagined stars so heavy light could not escape -- designed and built it, died in 1793 before using it, and it reached Cavendish second-hand through Francis Wollaston. T5c: what the number MEANT -- 5.5 times water is far denser than any surface rock (about 2.7), so the Earth must hide something much heavier deep inside: the first quantitative evidence for a dense metallic core.
source: Grokipedia 'Cavendish experiment' (read via browser); Wikipedia 'Cavendish experiment'; Wikipedia 'Schiehallion experiment'. Grokipedia and Wikipedia differ on the published density (5.48 vs the corrected 5.448) exactly as described in the accuracy rail; both agree Cavendish did not compute G.
framing_note: T1 keys the TELESCOPE-FROM-OUTSIDE -- the absurd lengths precision demands -- not a date. Accuracy rail #1: Cavendish did NOT measure the gravitational constant and never used the term; he measured the Earth's mean DENSITY and called the work 'weighing the world.' Any rung crediting him with G is wrong. Rail #2: his published 5.48 carries a later-found arithmetic error; his data give 5.448 -- state which number is which. Rail #3: the shyness anecdotes (the note to the housekeeper, the separate back staircase) are traditional contemporary reports -- frame as 'contemporaries said,' never as documented fact. Dinner-test payoff: T4a -- you can weigh the Earth by watching a hanging string lean toward a mountain. Distractor mine: the real rival routes and figures seriously held -- Schiehallion's 4.5, Newton's own Principia guess of five to six times water (remarkably good), Bouguer's earlier Chimborazo attempt in Peru, the seconds-pendulum method -- plus real adjacent names (Michell, Maskelyne, Hutton, Wollaston, Boys). Lane border: geography owns Earth's layered interior as a place-fact; science keys HOW the core was inferred from a single density number.
history_overlap: geography bank -- Earth's core/mantle structure as an earth-system fact. Science keys the INFERENCE (density 5.5 vs surface rock 2.7 implies a heavy interior), not the tour of the layers.

name: Foucault's pendulum: watching the Earth turn
scope: The afternoon an audience watched the planet rotate. T1: in 1851 Leon Foucault hung a 28-kg brass-coated lead bob on a 67-metre wire under the dome of the Pantheon in Paris, drew it back, and let go -- and over the next hours the plane of its swing visibly drifted away from where it had started (the hook: a crowd standing still, watching the Earth move). T2: nothing turned the pendulum. The bob kept swinging in the same plane in space; the floor, the building and Paris rotated underneath it. T3: the drift rate depends on WHERE you are -- at the Pantheon's latitude (about 49 N) the plane took roughly 32 hours for a full turn; at the North Pole it would take about 24 hours; at the equator it never turns at all, because the rate follows the sine of the latitude. T4a: the first version was tiny and private -- a 2-metre pendulum in Foucault's own cellar in January 1851, then a demonstration in the Meridian Room of the Paris Observatory in February, and only then the Pantheon. T4b: Foucault trained for medicine and abandoned it, and had no university physics post -- he was, in the eyes of the Academy, an instrument-maker and a journalist. T5a: why it mattered -- three centuries after Copernicus, every proof of Earth's rotation had been indirect and technical (stellar aberration, parallax, the eastward deflection of falling bodies); Foucault's was the first that an untrained person could simply WATCH happen. T5b: he didn't stop -- in 1852 he built and named the GYROSCOPE to show the same rotation with a spinning wheel, and in 1862 used a rotating mirror to measure light's speed at about 298,000 km/s. T5c: the original bob's end -- it hung in the Musee des Arts et Metiers until 6 April 2010, when the suspension cable snapped and the historic bob was irreparably damaged; a replica swings under the Pantheon dome today.
source: Wikipedia 'Foucault pendulum' (67 m wire, 28 kg bob, 31.8 h at 48 deg 52' N, Meridian Room February 1851, 2010 cable failure). Grokipedia's Foucault page could not be opened this session (WebFetch 403; the shared browser tabs were being reassigned by parallel agents mid-read) -- the build stage should check it first per source priority.
framing_note: T1 keys the CROWD WATCHING THE PLANE DRIFT, not a date. Accuracy rail: the Earth does not drag, twist or push the pendulum -- the bob conserves its plane and the observer's frame rotates beneath it; no rung may imply a force acting on the swing. Second rail: the Pantheon figure is about 32 hours (31.8 h), the pole is about 24 hours (a sidereal day), and at the equator the plane does NOT turn -- never say '24 hours everywhere.' Third rail: Foucault's widely quoted invitation ('you are invited to come see the Earth turn') must be sourced to a document before any rung uses it verbatim; paraphrase if it cannot be. Dinner-test payoff: T3 -- a kid can predict what a Foucault pendulum would do at his own latitude and then go find one in a science museum and check. Distractor mine: the real rival proofs of Earth's rotation that came before (Bradley's stellar aberration 1729, Bessel's stellar parallax 1838, the eastward deflection of dropped weights, trade-wind patterns) plus real adjacent names (Coriolis, Arago, Bessel). Lane border: geography owns the Pantheon as a Paris landmark and the Coriolis effect on weather systems; science keys the ROTATION PROOF and the frame-of-reference mechanism.
history_overlap: geography bank -- Paris landmarks (the Pantheon) and the Coriolis effect in atmospheric circulation. Science keys the pendulum as PROOF OF ROTATION and the sine-of-latitude mechanism, not the building or the weather.

name: Michelson-Morley: the most famous nothing
scope: The experiment that found nothing and changed everything. T1: in a basement in Cleveland in 1887, a heavy sandstone slab floated on a pool of liquid MERCURY so that a whole optical instrument could be turned by hand without a single jolt (the hook: an experiment floated on a metal that pours). T2: teach the ether -- physicists were certain light waves needed a medium the way sound needs air, a 'luminiferous ether' filling all space; if Earth plows through it at about 30 km/s, light should run measurably faster along one arm than the other. T3a: the 1881 solo attempt in Potsdam was too crude; the 1887 rebuild with Edward Morley folded the light path with multiple mirrors to about 11 metres of effective arm, boosting sensitivity roughly tenfold. T3b: the prediction was specific -- a shift of about 0.4 of a fringe as the instrument rotated. Michelson and Morley measured less than 0.02. T4a: Michelson considered it a FAILURE. He had built the most sensitive instrument on Earth to detect something and detected nothing, and spent years thinking he had botched it. T4b: the respectable rescue -- George FitzGerald and Hendrik Lorentz proposed that motion through the ether physically CONTRACTS an object along its direction of travel by exactly the amount needed to hide the effect; it was honest and testable, and its mathematics survived into relativity even though the ether did not. T5a: Einstein's move in 1905 was to stop explaining why the ether hides and instead throw it out, making the constancy of light's speed a starting postulate. T5b: a null result is not 'nothing' -- it is a NUMBER with an error bar. 'Less than 0.02 fringes against a predicted 0.4' is what excludes the ether wind; 'we measured nothing' and 'we did not measure' are opposite statements. T5c: it got challenged -- Dayton Miller ran thousands of Michelson-type observations at Mount Wilson through the 1920s and reported a small POSITIVE drift; the effect was eventually traced to temperature gradients in his apparatus. T5d: Michelson took the 1907 Nobel Prize -- the first American to win one in the sciences -- for his optical precision instruments, not for demolishing the ether.
source: Grokipedia 'Michelson-Morley experiment' (read via browser: 1887 Case School of Applied Science, mercury-float mounting, ~11 m effective arm, predicted ~0.40 fringe shift vs observed <0.02, observations 8-12 July 1887, Fizeau 1851 and Airy 1871 as the prior attempts, Dayton Miller's 1920s repeats).
framing_note: T1 keys the MERCURY FLOAT -- a piece of apparatus a ten-year-old can picture -- and 'ether' MUST be taught at T2 before any rung tests it. Accuracy rail #1: do NOT claim the experiment 'proved Einstein right' or that Einstein built relativity on it; Einstein's own statements about its influence are inconsistent, so a rung must say the null result cleared the road, never that it caused the theory. Rail #2: the bound is 'less than about 0.02 fringes against a predicted 0.4,' not 'exactly zero.' Dinner-test payoff: T4a -- the most celebrated experiment in physics was, to the man who ran it, a failure. Distractor mine: the graveyard of respectable ether models is the richest in the sub-strand -- stationary ether, Stokes' full ether drag, Fresnel's partial drag coefficient (confirmed by Fizeau's 1851 flowing-water tubes), the FitzGerald-Lorentz contraction -- plus real adjacent experiments (Airy's water-filled telescope, Trouton-Noble, Kennedy-Thorndike). Never let a distractor secretly be the truth. Lane border: PHILOSOPHY owns falsification as an epistemological doctrine; science keys what a good TEST looks like and what an upper bound actually buys you.
history_overlap: philosophy bank -- falsifiability / how a theory gets refuted, as a Popperian seminar move. Science keys the WORKING PRACTICE: a specific numeric prediction (0.4 fringes) versus a measured bound (<0.02), and what a null result is worth.

name: Millikan's oil drops and the slow crawl to truth
scope: Measuring one electron -- and the psychology of everyone who measured it next. T2a: in 1909 at the University of Chicago, Robert Millikan sprayed a fine mist of OIL between two charged metal plates and watched single droplets through a microscope, tuning the voltage until one droplet hung dead still in mid-air, its electric pull exactly balancing its weight. T2b: why oil and not water -- earlier attempts by J.J. Thomson and H.A. Wilson used water droplets that EVAPORATED while being watched, changing mass mid-measurement. T3a: the result that mattered was not the number but the PATTERN -- every droplet's charge came out as a whole-number multiple of one base amount, so electric charge comes in indivisible lumps. T3b: his published value was about 1.592e-19 coulombs, roughly 0.6% below today's exactly-defined 1.602176634e-19 C. T4a: WHY he was low -- he used a slightly wrong value for the VISCOSITY of air, which enters the calculation that turns a droplet's fall speed into its size. A wrong supporting constant, not sloppy observing. T4b: the coda -- in his 1974 Caltech commencement address 'Cargo Cult Science,' Richard Feynman pointed out that measurements of the electron's charge after Millikan crept UPWARD in small steps instead of jumping to the right answer, because an experimenter who got a much higher number went hunting for what was wrong with his own apparatus, and stopped hunting once the number sat near Millikan's. T4c: Millikan's 1923 Nobel was for the charge AND for confirming Einstein's photoelectric equation -- an experiment he undertook expecting to DISPROVE the light-quantum idea, and which instead confirmed it in detail. T5a: Feynman's rule for the whole problem -- the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. T5b: the modern fix is BLIND ANALYSIS: real physics collaborations now hide the final answer from their own analysts (a secret offset added to the data, or scrambled samples) until the method is frozen, precisely so 'does it match the accepted value?' cannot steer the work. T5c: the data-selection charge -- Gerald Holton found in 1978 that Millikan's notebooks held more drops than he published, annotated with remarks like 'beautiful'; later review concluded he reported drops from complete observation runs and stated his selection rule in print. The honest verdict is 'he selected, and he said so,' not 'he faked it.' T5d: Harvey Fletcher, the graduate student who did much of the work, wrote that Millikan required sole authorship on the key paper as a condition of his PhD -- and kept it quiet until after his own death.
source: Grokipedia 'Oil drop experiment' (read via browser: 1909 start, oil chosen over water to defeat evaporation, up to 6,000 V/cm, e = 4.774e-10 esu ~ 1.592e-19 C, charge quantization, 1923 Nobel, the later data-selection revelations); Wikipedia 'Oil drop experiment' (Harvey Fletcher authorship, the air-viscosity cause, Holton 1978 and Goodstein's review, the Feynman 'Cargo Cult Science' passage). Feynman's quotation must be checked against the published text of the 1974 Caltech commencement address before use.
framing_note: THE epistemic flagship of the sub-strand -- vision_mandated because it turns squarely on the bank's stance that social pressure and deference to an eminent result can bend even honest measurement, and that the first scientific virtue is skepticism toward your OWN answer. The bank PRESENTS, never preaches: rungs report what Feynman observed and what Holton found; no rung calls Millikan a fraud. Accuracy rail #1: on the data-selection charge, the resolved verdict is that Millikan excluded drops but published his selection criterion and no fraud was established -- a rung asserting he faked data is WRONG. Rail #2: any Feynman line must be the documented 'Cargo Cult Science' wording; never invent a Feynman quote. Rail #3: his error came from the air-viscosity value and his result is about 0.6% low -- do not inflate it. Dinner-test payoff: T4b -- everyone crept toward the truth in small respectable steps because nobody wanted to disagree with Millikan too much at once. Distractor mine: real rival measurements and real rival mechanisms -- Thomson's water-cloud method, Townsend's ionized-cloud estimate, H.A. Wilson's field-balanced water drops, and above all Felix Ehrenhaft, a serious physicist who spent years insisting his own drops showed fractional 'subelectrons' and that charge was NOT quantized -- plus the real wrong causes for Millikan's offset (evaporation, plate-voltage calibration, Brownian motion). Lane border: PHILOSOPHY owns confirmation bias as a named concept; science keys the WORKING PRACTICE that answers it -- blind analysis and stated selection rules.
history_overlap: philosophy bank -- confirmation bias / theory-ladenness of observation as epistemology. Science keys the concrete case (the post-Millikan creep in published electron-charge values) and the practical countermeasure (blind analysis), not the philosophical concept.

name: Harrison's sea clocks and the longitude prize
scope: A carpenter, a watch, and a board that would not pay. T1: sailors could read their latitude off the Sun, but nobody could find longitude -- and in October 1707 four British warships drove onto the rocks of the Scilly Isles at night with the loss of well over a thousand men, because the fleet did not know how far west it was. T2a: the trick is a CLOCK. Local noon is when the Sun peaks where you stand; carry a clock still telling home time and the gap between the two tells you how far around the world you have come, at fifteen degrees per hour. T2b: Parliament's Longitude Act of 1714 posted 20,000 pounds -- a fortune -- for a method good to half a degree after a voyage to the West Indies. T3a: why no clock could do it -- pendulums are useless on a heaving deck, and metal springs and rods change length with heat and cold, so a clock that kept perfect time in London gained or lost minutes in the tropics. T3b: John Harrison was a self-taught Yorkshire joiner who built his first clocks almost entirely of WOOD, using lignum vitae, a timber so oily it lubricates itself and needs no oil to gum up. T4a: his gridiron pendulum paired brass and iron rods whose different expansions cancelled each other, so heat could not change the effective length. T4b: his grasshopper escapement kicked the movement along with almost no friction and no lubricant at all, because the oils of the age thickened in cold and thinned in heat. T4c: the surprise turn -- after three enormous sea CLOCKS (H1, H2, H3) over some twenty-five years, Harrison abandoned the big-machine idea entirely and produced H4, a five-inch watch. T5a: on the Jamaica trial of 1761-62 H4 was out by about 1.25 minutes of time after 81 days at sea -- roughly one nautical mile of longitude. The Board of Longitude called it luck and demanded a second trial. T5b: the rival was no crank -- Nevil Maskelyne's lunar-distance method used the Moon's position against the stars as a natural clock; it demanded hours of computation and clear skies, but it cost nothing to replace if dropped overboard, and it was genuinely used at sea alongside chronometers for a century. T5c: Harrison never won the prize. In 1773, aged 80, he received 8,750 pounds by a separate act of Parliament after his appeal reached George III, who had personally tested H5 at Kew for ten weeks; the official 20,000-pound award was never given to anyone. T5d: the vindication came after his death -- Larcum Kendall's K1, a copy of H4, sailed with Captain Cook, and Cook's Pacific charts are accurate because of it.
source: Wikipedia 'John Harrison' (Longitude Act 1714 and the 20,000-pound scale, gridiron pendulum, grasshopper escapement, H1 Lisbon trial 1735, H4 completed 1759, the 1761-62 Jamaica trial error of ~1.25 minutes over 81 days, Maskelyne's negative report and the lunar-distance rivalry, George III's ten-week Kew test of H5, the 8,750-pound parliamentary award of 1773, K1 with Cook, K2 on the Bounty, Harrison's death 1776, and the modern historiographic pushback on Dava Sobel's villain-Maskelyne framing). Grokipedia's Harrison page was not reachable this session (WebFetch 403; shared browser tabs contended) -- check it first at build time.
framing_note: T1 keys the SHIPWRECK -- the human cost that created the prize -- never a date; T2a must teach clock-equals-longitude before any rung tests it. Accuracy rail #1: Harrison NEVER won the 20,000-pound prize and neither did anyone else; the 1773 payment was a separate parliamentary act for 8,750 pounds. A rung saying 'he finally won the prize' is flatly wrong. Rail #2: the popular villain-Maskelyne narrative is contested by modern historians -- lunar distances was a real, working, cheaper solution and the Board's insistence on reproducibility from a six-year handmade watch was not absurd. Present institution-versus-outsider WITH the Board's genuine objection stated; do not cartoon it, and do not turn the ladder into a sermon. Rail #3: Scilly death-toll estimates vary widely in the sources (roughly 1,400 to over 2,000) -- hedge the figure. Dinner-test payoff: T2a -- a kid can find his own longitude with a watch left on home time and a stick's shortest shadow. Distractor mine: the rival longitude schemes seriously proposed at the time -- lunar distances, timing the eclipses of Jupiter's moons (Galileo's method, unusable on a rolling deck), magnetic-variation charts, dead reckoning, and the genuinely proposed 'powder of sympathy' wounded-dog scheme. Lane border: HISTORY owns the Royal Navy, empire and Cook's voyages as narrative; science keys the CLOCK PROBLEM and the mechanisms (gridiron, grasshopper, self-lubricating wood) that solved it.
history_overlap: history bank -- the 1707 Scilly naval disaster, the Longitude Act as a piece of British parliamentary history, and Captain Cook's voyages of exploration. Science keys the physics of a clock at sea and Harrison's specific mechanisms, not the naval or imperial narrative. Also geography bank -- Greenwich and the prime meridian.

name: Mechain's error and the metre cut from the Earth
scope: A unit carved out of the planet, and the mistake its maker took to his grave. T1: the metre was not chosen for convenience -- it was cut from the Earth itself, defined in 1791 as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator along the meridian running through Paris. T2: to find that distance, Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Mechain spent seven years triangulating the arc from Dunkirk to Barcelona -- through the French Revolution, hauling brass instruments up church towers while suspicious citizens took them for spies and had them arrested. T3a: the instrument that made it possible was Borda's repeating circle, which let an observer stack the same angle over and over so that the random error of any single sighting averaged away. T3b: the definition the Academy REJECTED was the seconds pendulum -- the length of a pendulum that ticks once per second -- thrown out partly because it depends on local gravity and would therefore differ from town to town. T4: Mechain's secret. At Barcelona he measured the latitude from two different stations and the two results DISAGREED by about three arcseconds. He could not explain it, so he concealed it, reworked his notebooks, and it tormented him for the rest of his life; he died of malaria in 1804 on a return expedition to Spain, still trying to put it right. T5a: he was not careless -- the discrepancy came largely from the deflection of the vertical: nearby mountains pull a plumb line sideways, so 'straight down' does not point exactly at the Earth's centre. Mechain had stumbled onto a real physical effect nobody had budgeted for. T5b: the outcome -- the metre of the Archives is about 0.2 mm SHORT of the quarter-meridian definition it was supposed to embody, and the world kept it anyway, because a standard's job is to be SHARED, not to be perfect. T4b: the same Revolution decreed a decimal clock of ten-hour days and hundred-minute hours, and a decimal calendar. Those died within years; the metre lived.
source: Wikipedia 'History of the metre' (the 1791 quarter-meridian definition, the Dunkirk-to-Barcelona survey 1792-99, Mechain's concealed Barcelona discrepancy and his death of malaria in 1804, the metre des Archives of 1799, the ~0.2 mm shortfall attributed to vertical deflection at the southern end of the arc, and the 1889 / 1960 krypton-86 / 1983 speed-of-light redefinitions). Ken Alder, 'The Measure of All Things' (2002) is the standard secondary account of the Mechain episode and should be the build stage's corroborating source. Grokipedia's metre/Mechain pages were not reachable this session (WebFetch 403) -- check first at build time.
framing_note: T1 inverts the wonder -- the astonishing claim (your ruler is a slice of the planet) goes in the STEM, and the exact form of the definition is the knowable answer. Accuracy rail: Mechain did not fabricate a result to deceive -- he concealed a discrepancy he could not explain, and modern analysis shows the anomaly was largely real physics (deflection of the vertical), not incompetence. No rung may call him a fraud; the wonder is a careful man broken by an honest anomaly. Second rail: '0.2 mm short' is short OF ITS OWN quarter-meridian definition -- say what it is short of, or the claim is meaningless. Dinner-test payoff: T5b -- the most carefully made unit in history is measurably wrong and we kept it on purpose. Distractor mine: the real rival definitions live at the time (the seconds pendulum, a fraction of the equator rather than the meridian, the toise du Perou, a king's-arm length) plus real adjacent commission names (Borda, Lagrange, Laplace, Legendre, Lavoisier). Lane border: HISTORY owns the Revolution as politics and the Republican calendar as revolutionary culture; science keys the SURVEY, the repeating circle, and the physical anomaly Mechain found.
history_overlap: history bank -- the French Revolution, including the metric system as a revolutionary project and the Republican calendar. Science keys the meridian SURVEY, Borda's repeating circle and Mechain's concealed discrepancy, not the politics.

name: The day the last artifact died
scope: A CONCEPT ladder: why a unit should be anchored to something nature cannot change. T1: until 2019 the kilogram was a THING -- a cylinder of platinum-iridium about the size of a plum, sitting in a vault outside Paris behind three locks whose keys were held by three different people, and it was taken out and compared to its sister copies only three times in 130 years. T2: the problem with defining a unit as an object -- over about a century, this prototype and its official copies drifted apart by roughly 50 micrograms, about the mass of a fingerprint, and nobody could say WHICH had changed, because by definition the prototype was always exactly one kilogram. It could not be weighed; it could only be compared. T3a: the other units had already escaped. The second stopped being a fraction of a day in 1967 and became 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a caesium-133 atom. T3b: the metre stopped being a bar in 1983 and became the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second -- which means the speed of light is no longer measured at all. It is DEFINED, and every improvement in measurement now refines the metre instead. T4a: the kilogram's escape needed a machine -- the Kibble balance weighs a mass against a precisely known electromagnetic force, tying mass to the Planck constant through electrical measurement. T4b: a rival route came at it from the opposite end -- the Avogadro project COUNTED the atoms in a sphere of isotopically pure silicon-28, among the roundest objects ever manufactured. T4c: the two routes had to AGREE before the change was permitted -- a redefinition is only safe when two independent methods with entirely different error sources land on the same number. T5a: on 20 May 2019 the SI fixed the Planck constant at exactly 6.62607015e-34 J s, and with it the elementary charge, the Boltzmann constant and the Avogadro constant. Those numbers lost their error bars, because they stopped being measurements and became definitions. T5b: what it buys -- any properly equipped laboratory on Earth, or on Mars, can now realize a kilogram from scratch without ever touching, borrowing or shipping a French artifact.
source: Wikipedia 'International Prototype of the Kilogram' (90% platinum / 10% iridium, ~39 mm cylinder, sanctioned 1889, three independently controlled keys, six sister copies, ~50 microgram divergence from the replicas over the last century, periodic verifications in 1889, 1948 and 1989, retirement 20 May 2019) and Wikipedia '2019 revision of the SI' (h, e, k and N_A fixed exactly; Kibble balance and silicon-28 Avogadro sphere as the two reconciled routes; the second and metre already constant-based since 1967 and 1983). Grokipedia not reachable this session (WebFetch 403) -- check first at build time.
framing_note: The sub-strand's CONCEPT/THEME ladder, carrying its analytic T4/T5 ceiling: one method-idea (anchor the unit to an unchangeable constant) traced across the second, the metre and the kilogram. Accuracy rail #1: the drift figure is the divergence BETWEEN the prototype and its copies (about 50 micrograms over roughly a century) and its direction is genuinely unresolved -- never assert 'Le Grand K lost mass,' and never say it 'became lighter than a kilogram,' which was definitionally impossible under the old system. That impossibility IS the wonder, so state it exactly. Rail #2: 2019 redefined the kilogram, ampere, kelvin and mole -- the second and metre were already constant-based; a rung claiming 2019 redefined the metre is wrong. Teach 'artifact standard' and 'physical constant' before testing either. Dinner-test payoff: T2 -- the object that defined the kilogram was the one object in the world that could not be weighed. Distractor mine: real superseded standards (the metre des Archives bar, the 1960 krypton-86 wavelength metre, the 1795 kilogram as the mass of a litre of water at its densest, the mean-solar-day second) and the two real rival realization routes (Kibble balance versus the silicon-28 sphere). No sister-bank overlap.

name: The transits of Venus: the first worldwide experiment
scope: Nations at war sending astronomers to the ends of the Earth to time a black dot. T1: twice in a lifetime, and then not again for over a century, Venus crosses the face of the Sun as a small black dot -- and for the transits of 1761 and 1769, governments that were actively at war with one another dispatched hundreds of observers to Siberia, Newfoundland, Madagascar and the South Pacific to time it. T2: the plan was Edmond Halley's, published in 1716, and he knew he would be long dead before it could be used -- observers far apart on Earth see Venus cross a slightly different chord of the Sun, and the difference in crossing TIMES yields the angle, which yields the distance to the Sun. T3a: what was at stake -- astronomers already knew the exact SHAPE of the solar system, because Kepler's laws gave every planet's distance in units of the Earth-Sun distance. What nobody had was the SCALE. One good transit would supply the ruler for the entire universe. T3b: Captain Cook's first voyage was, officially, a transit expedition -- the Endeavour sailed to Tahiti so that Cook and the astronomer Charles Green could time the 1769 crossing from a headland still called Point Venus. T4a: Guillaume Le Gentil's disaster -- he left France in 1760 for India, was blocked by war, and was still at sea on transit day in 1761, which was useless because a precise sighting cannot be taken from a rolling deck. He stayed abroad eight more years for the 1769 transit, built an observatory at Pondicherry, and on the morning of the event a cloud arrived and sat over the Sun for its duration. T4b: the problem nobody predicted -- the BLACK DROP EFFECT: as Venus's disc meets the Sun's edge it appears to stretch into a clinging teardrop, so observers could not agree within seconds when 'contact' occurred, and the seconds were the whole measurement. It is now understood as diffraction blur in the telescope combined with the darkening of the Sun's limb. T4c: one real discovery did come out of 1761 -- Mikhail Lomonosov, watching from St Petersburg, reported a bright arc around Venus's edge at contact and inferred that Venus has an ATMOSPHERE. T5a: the payoff -- Lalande combined the 1761 and 1769 data to about 153 million km, roughly 2% high against today's 149.6 million; Simon Newcomb's later analysis of all four nineteenth-century transits gave 149.59 million. T5b: the rhythm is strange -- transits come in pairs eight years apart, separated by gaps of 105 and 121 years. The last pair was 2004 and 2012; the next is 2117, so nobody now alive gets another chance. T5c: the method is obsolete -- we now bounce RADAR off Venus and time the echo, which pinned the distance far tighter than any transit, and in 2012 the astronomical unit was simply defined as an exact number of metres.
source: Wikipedia 'Transit of Venus' (Halley's 1716 parallax proposal; the 1761 and 1769 expeditions to Siberia, Newfoundland and Madagascar; Cook and Charles Green at Point Venus, Tahiti; Maximilian Hell, Chappe d'Auteroche, Mason and Dixon at the Cape; Le Gentil's eight-plus years of travel and his losses on return; the black drop effect; Lalande's 153 +/- 1 million km, Hell's 151.7 million, Newcomb's 149.59 +/- 0.31 million; the modern 149.6 million km). framing_note: T1 keys the WORLDWIDE COORDINATION BETWEEN ENEMIES, not a date; parallax must be taught before T2 tests it. Accuracy rail #1: tell Le Gentil precisely -- he missed 1761 because he was still at sea (a sighting from a moving deck is worthless) and 1769 because of cloud over Pondicherry. The popular epilogue about his estate being divided and his wife remarrying is variously reported, so key the CLOUD and leave the domestic coda out unless the build can source it. Rail #2: the black drop effect is NOT caused by Venus's atmosphere -- that explanation was widely believed and is wrong; it is an optical artefact of diffraction and limb darkening. Rail #3: Lomonosov's priority for the atmosphere inference is genuinely contested in the history-of-science literature; write 'reported' and let the wonder be the observation, not the award. Dinner-test payoff: T5b -- the next transit is 2117, and nobody reading this will see one. Distractor mine: the wrong solar distances seriously held (Ptolemy's roughly 1,200 Earth radii, Kepler's lower bound, Cassini's 1672 Mars-parallax figure of about 138 million km) and the real rival scale methods (Mars opposition parallax, the aberration of light, the asteroid Eros campaign of 1900-01, modern radar ranging). Lane border: HISTORY owns Cook's voyages as exploration and empire; GEOGRAPHY owns Tahiti as a place; science keys the PARALLAX METHOD and the timing problem that defeated it.
history_overlap: history bank -- Captain Cook's voyages and the Endeavour as an exploration narrative; geography bank -- Tahiti as a Pacific place. Science keys the parallax METHOD, the black-drop timing failure and the derived astronomical unit, not the voyage story or the island.

name: Romer's late moon
scope: The first time anyone caught light taking its time. T2: at the Paris Observatory in 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Romer noticed that Jupiter's innermost moon Io -- which slips into Jupiter's shadow like clockwork every 42 and a half hours -- was running LATE. Over months the eclipses fell further and further behind the tables, then caught back up, on a yearly rhythm. T3a: Romer's explanation had nothing to do with Io. The eclipses arrive late when Earth is on the far side of its orbit from Jupiter, because the LIGHT has farther to travel. Light is not instantaneous. T3b: the move that made it science -- in the summer of 1676 he announced in advance that a particular Io event that November would occur about ten minutes later than the published tables predicted, and it did. T4a: what Romer actually delivered was a TIME, not a speed -- roughly 22 minutes for light to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit (the true figure is about 16.7). He never published a value in leagues or miles, because nobody yet knew the size of the orbit well enough -- exactly the number the Venus transits would later supply. T4b: Christiaan Huygens took Romer's time, plugged in the best orbit size available, and got about 220,000 km/s -- some 26% low, and the first finite number for the speed of light in history. T5a: the resistance came from inside the building -- Giovanni Domenico Cassini, Romer's own superior and the most respected astronomer in Europe, who had helped publicize the anomaly, never accepted the finite-speed explanation and preferred to blame irregularities in Io's own motion. T5b: what finally settled it was a completely different measurement -- James Bradley's 1729 discovery of stellar ABERRATION, in which stars appear shifted by the combination of Earth's motion and light's finite speed, the way rain slants into the face of a running child. Bradley found it while hunting for something else entirely (stellar parallax) and failing to find it.
source: Wikipedia "Romer's determination of the speed of light" (Paris Observatory 1676, Io's 42.5-hour period, the varying eclipse intervals, Cassini's 22 August 1676 announcement to the Academy, the predicted ~10-minute delay confirmed by the 9 November 1676 emergence, the ~22-minute orbital-diameter crossing time, Romer publishing no speed value, Huygens' ~220,000 km/s against the true 299,792, Cassini's lifelong skepticism, and Bradley's 1729 aberration result of 8 min 13 s). framing_note: T2 keys the MOON RUNNING LATE -- a checkable phenomenon, since a kid with binoculars and a published Io-eclipse timetable can actually watch Jupiter swallow a moon on schedule. Accuracy rail #1: Romer did NOT publish a speed of light; he gave a crossing TIME (about 22 minutes for the diameter of Earth's orbit, against the true ~16.7) and Huygens converted it into a speed. Any rung crediting Romer with '220,000 km/s' is wrong. Rail #2: the 1676 announcement-and-confirmation chronology is fiddly in the sources, so key the FACT of a successful advance prediction rather than pinning a precise date pairing. Dinner-test payoff: T3b -- he told them in advance exactly how late the moon would be, and it was. Distractor mine: the rival explanations genuinely live at the time (irregularities in Io's own orbit, refraction in Jupiter's atmosphere, errors in the Jovian tables) plus the real neighbouring attempts on light's speed -- Galileo's lantern-and-hilltop trial, which established only that light was 'extraordinarily rapid,' and later Fizeau's toothed wheel of 1849 and Foucault's rotating mirror. Internal lane border: the bank's earth-and-space sub-strand owns Jupiter and the Galilean moons as objects; this ladder keys the TIMING ANOMALY and the finite-speed inference.
